You pass if the recursion is right, the counts are there, and you say that the same sub-problem is recomputed many times and name overlapping sub-problems. A correct recursion with a vague "it is slow" is a partial pass. Missing that
is 1, or answering with a formula you cannot justify, is a fail.

Dynamic programming solves a problem by answering each of its smaller sub-problems exactly once and reusing that answer everywhere it's needed again, instead of rederiving it. It only applies when two properties hold. The sub-problems have to overlap: a plain recursion asks the same small question many times over, which is what climbing n steps one or two at a time shows, because counting the calls a naive recursion makes reveals the same smaller counts computed again and again. And the problem needs optimal substructure: the answer for n has to be built from the answers to smaller inputs, and those smaller answers can't depend on how you got to them.

The problem this solves is exactly that waste. A recursion with no memory of what it has already answered turns a question with only n distinct sub-problems into one with an exponential number of calls, because every path down the call tree recomputes shared work from scratch.

The mechanism is to store each sub-problem's answer once known, and there are two ways to do it. Memoisation keeps the original recursion and adds a lookup: before recursing, it checks whether this input is already answered, and if so returns the stored value instead of descending further. This is top-down, because it starts at the question actually asked and only computes what that needs. A table drops the recursion entirely and fills the sub-problems in an order that guarantees each one's inputs already exist, which is bottom-up and needs no call stack at all. Once the transition only reads a fixed number of earlier states, the table can shrink to a couple of variables, trading O(n) space for O(1) at the cost of no longer recovering which choices produced the answer.
What it costs, unannounced, is the size of the numbers. A counting recurrence like this one grows fast, so an accumulator that looks fine in every test run by hand overflows a plain
a few steps further on, and the wraparound is silent unless a sanitizer is watching for it. The fix is accumulating in a 64-bit type from the first line, not after something breaks.

You meet this in the interview question itself: explain overlapping sub-problems using the number of ways to climb a flight of stairs, where the call count of the naive recursion against the same count once each answer is stored is the proof.

The general rule is that a table needs to keep only as far back as its recurrence reaches, so a recurrence over a two-dimensional table that reads the previous row keeps one row rather than all of them.

c.v: Two things are worth saying about when this applies at all. If the sub-problems do not overlap, memoising them wins nothing and the problem is ordinary divide and conquer: merge sort splits into two halves that share no element, which is why nobody memoises it. If the answer to a sub-problem depends on the route taken to reach it, there is no optimal substructure and a table over that state is wrong rather than slow, which is the trap in problems with a constraint such as "at most k turns": the state has to include the turns used so far, and the table gains a dimension.

Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so without the sanitizer the value silently wraps negative and the answer is wrong from n = 46 on. Counting problems overflow sooner than anyone expects, which is why the accumulators on this page are

The transition is where this differs from the cold check, and it is the difference between counting and optimising. Stairs added the two cases because it wanted how many. This takes the smaller of the two because it wants the cheapest, and a problem that wants the largest takes

The three implementations agree on every input, and the memoised one made 19 calls for ten levels against the table's eleven cells, of which its loop writes nine and the two base cases arrive already zeroed. The memoised version costs more calls than the table costs cells, because it also calls into the base cases and into slots that are already filled. Both are O(n). The table is the one to ship: it has no recursion and therefore no depth, and the two-variable version drops its memory to O(1). What the two-variable version cannot do is say which route it took, and the exercise below is where that matters.

The walk back is the part the exercise is really about.

That works because the table holds enough information to replay the decision, and the two-variable version does not: it keeps the totals and throws the history away. So the space reduction is not free, and the question to ask before applying it is whether the caller wants the answer or the plan. A robot that wants to know how much energy it can collect takes the two variables. A robot that has to drive to the bays needs the indices.

This is the third problem on this page with the same recurrence shape: one state per position, a transition that looks back a fixed distance, and a reduction to a couple of variables. Stairs added the candidates, the pallet climb took the smallest, this one takes the largest. When an interview problem is a sequence and the question mentions a maximum, a minimum or a count subject to a local constraint, try that shape first: write the state in one sentence, and if the transition only needs a fixed number of earlier states, you have a linear solution.
